mcqs.question: Two teams build functionally identical features. Team A designs it to only deploy all-at-once with no partial state; Team B designs it to support a gradual rollout from the start. Per this topic, what's true of the two designs?
options: Team A's design is riskier, even though the end state is identical, because it can't be exposed gradually or turned off in pieces
The two designs carry identical risk, since the shipped feature is the same either way
Team B's design is necessarily slower to build, which offsets any rollout safety benefit
Rollout strategy is purely an operational concern and doesn't reflect back on the design itself
mcqs.explanation: Whether a design supports partial exposure and instant disablement is itself a design property, not just a deployment detail — so the all-at-once design is riskier despite an identical end state. The topic explicitly argues rollout is part of the design, not a separate operational afterthought.

mcqs.question: What does a feature flag primarily let you decouple during a rollout?
options: The database schema from the application code
Deploying the code (getting it onto production machines) from releasing it (users actually experiencing it)
The frontend from the backend
Testing from staging entirely
mcqs.explanation: A feature flag's core value is separating deploy from release: code can sit on production dark, then be released gradually or disabled instantly, all without a new deploy. It isn't primarily about schema, frontend/backend separation, or staging.

mcqs.question: A new recommendation engine returns technically-valid but subtly wrong results — no errors, no latency spike, just different answers. Which rollout technique is best suited to catch this before real users see it?
options: A percentage-based phased rollout alone
A blue-green deployment alone
Shadow traffic, comparing the new path's output against the current system's without returning it to users
A feature flag with no comparison mechanism
mcqs.explanation: Shadow traffic is specifically good at catching output-correctness bugs with no error signal, because it compares real traffic's results side by side without exposing users to either. A phased rollout or a bare flag would only catch this once it caused a measurable metric regression, if at all.

mcqs.question: Per this topic's comparison, what does shadow traffic fail to catch that canary release can?
options: Silent wrong-output bugs with no error signal
Bugs that show up under real traffic patterns at small scale, including actual user impact
Schema migration mistakes
Rollback complexity
mcqs.explanation: Canary exposes real user traffic to the new path at small scale, surfacing issues that only show up with genuine user impact, which shadow traffic can't do since it never returns results to users. Shadow traffic is the one better at catching silent wrong-output bugs, the reverse of this question's framing.

mcqs.question: A team says "we tested thoroughly in staging, so we don't need a kill switch." What's the flaw in this reasoning?
options: Thorough staging tests reduce the odds of a problem but don't substitute for an instant, no-deploy way to disable the new behavior if something still goes wrong
Staging tests are only useful for frontend changes, not backend ones
A kill switch is only needed if the team has low confidence in the change
Kill switches are unnecessary once a phased rollout is in place
mcqs.explanation: Staging traffic never fully matches production's data shapes, concurrency, and edge cases, so thorough testing lowers risk without eliminating the need for a fast, deploy-free way to turn a bad change off. Confidence level and having a phased rollout both address different concerns than an instant kill switch does.
